paragraphs.heading: The small tides of the month
paragraphs.text: Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea, driven mainly by the gravity of the Moon and the Sun. Many shores get two high tides and two low tides each day. The height gap between high and low water over about half a day is called the range, and it is not fixed: it grows and shrinks over a two-week cycle. A neap tide is the low point of that cycle, when the range is at its smallest.

paragraphs.heading: Why neaps happen
paragraphs.text: Neap tides arrive at the first-quarter and third-quarter moon. At those times the Sun and Moon are 90° apart as seen from Earth, a position called quadrature. The Sun's tidal force then works partly against the Moon's and cancels some of it. After this position, neap tides are sometimes called quadrature tides.

paragraphs.heading: The opposite of spring tides
paragraphs.text: Around new moon and full moon the picture flips. The Sun, Moon and Earth then form a line, the Sun's tidal force adds to the Moon's, and the range is at its largest; this is a spring tide. Spring tides bring higher highs, lower lows, briefer slack water and stronger currents than average. Neaps, by contrast, bring milder tidal conditions. Roughly seven days separate a spring tide from the next neap.

paragraphs.heading: A fitting name
paragraphs.text: The word neap comes from Anglo-Saxon and means without the power. It suits the moment when the Sun is partly cancelling the Moon's pull and the tide's range is at its smallest. People sometimes just call these days neaps.

paragraphs.heading: Average neap levels
paragraphs.text: Mean high water neaps is the average of the two high tides on neap-tide days. Mean low water neaps is the average of the two low tides on those same days. Mean high water springs and mean low water springs are worked out the same way, from the two highs or the two lows on spring-tide days.
